doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Black bands, entertainment and Dizzy's and Miles's choices
summary: Why musicians had to entertain: Ellington, Armstrong, Waller, Dizzy's failed big band, and Miles turning his back on audiences.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: is these guys are gifted they’re geniuses, but somehow or other it’s also natural and they’re different. They don’t need to be educated and they just came full blown from the head of Zeus — and French people particularly had that kind of attitude. And that ain’t the way it is, or was. And the facts are that the society at the time said white or black, if you wanted to make a living playing this kind of music you must entertain with it. You can’t just stand up there and play music to listen to. That’s not what it’s about. That’s all later when they decided it was an art. But I mean all the bands had a show. Even Benny Goodman, he had show business features to it. Although Benny got away with less than most. And the black bands, they all, even Duke, I mean Duke, well he was a genius because he was a virtuoso social person. He knew how to play the music exactly as he wanted to play it and make them think he’s entertaining them. I don’t know how he pulled this off but he did. Even though that’s another subject. But he never lost his dignity. But a lot of black guys were — now Louis Armstrong, you know he caught a lot of flack for the so-called Uncle — but he wasn’t really Uncle Tom, that’s another—
No. And he liked what he was doing, right?

He liked what he was doing. That’s another subject we won’t go into. But to give you a general answer I mean whether it was Fats Waller singing, I mean I think if he wanted to he, I mean he was a master pianist, I’m sure he enjoyed singing, but all that junk he had to sing, I mean there’s a lot of cynicism there. He’s making fun of all these songs. I think there’s no pat theories about it because — and I make statements like this and at the same time I’m talking like this I’m thinking of Dizzy Gillespie, the purest improviser, I mean didn’t compromise a note but my God he was like a latter day Louis jumping around and he’s clowning and he’s joking. So he’s like an exception, right? And he realized — well what I think he did was when you make a mark like that he probably figured look I came up with the new music, now I’ve got to eat. And the big band was a failure, financially. He lost his shirt, got ripped off. So I guess that must have been a turning point where he said I’ve got to do something, work all the time, so he had his little quintet and he’s singing “Eat More Meat, Pete” or whatever the heck it was “Pete eat More,” and all those things, and on the other hand some guys slightly younger, Miles, I’m not going to do that. Miles was a spoiled rich kid. So he could afford to do that. So everybody’s got a story so it’s a little bit dangerous for me to generalize. But to make a broad brush statement which is before Charlie Parker and Dizzy came up with those historic records and the music got a real foothold, you had to entertain on some level. And the music they were making was a statement about that, where they took it to extremes, where Miles turned his back on the audience and all that.
And the response from the audience was predictable, wasn’t it?
Yeah but they loved it. They used to go and see if he was going to show up?
